title: Coherent Control of an Embedded Bound State Without a Spectral Gap
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) can confine photonic excitations in open systems without conventional cavities or band gaps, making them natural candidates for long-lived quantum storage and single-photon control. Their use is limited, however, by two obstacles: they are dark to incident photons, and they lack spectral-gap protection from the surrounding continuum. We overcome both limitations in a giant atom coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide using two temporal control knobs. Atomic-frequency modulation breaks and restores the destructive-interference condition, enabling deterministic capture and release of mode-matched single photons. Coupling modulation instead preserves the BIC condition while tuning the atomic and photonic weights of the stored state. A key result is that this embedded state can nevertheless be controlled adiabatically despite the absence of a spectral gap, with an intrinsic leakage probability linear in the ramp rate. By separating radiative access from BIC-preserving deformation, the protocol turns a dark BIC into a single-photon memory whose fidelity is set by the intrinsic continuum-induced leakage law, providing a route to embedded-state control in open photonic platforms.
summary: This paper presents a method to coherently control an embedded bound state (BIC) in a giant atom coupled to a waveguide, overcoming the limitation that BICs lack spectral gap protection. By employing two temporal control knobs—frequency and coupling modulation—the authors show that deterministic single-photon memory operation is possible through adiabatic evolution, with leakage scaling linearly rather than quadratically with the ramp rate.
main_problem: The challenge is achieving coherent control of an embedded bound state (BIC) that lacks a spectral gap, which limits its use as a reliable quantum memory in open photonic systems.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that adiabatic control is possible even without a spectral gap, showing the intrinsic leakage probability scales linearly with the ramp rate ($	ext{P}_{	ext{leak}} \propto \gamma$).
method: The study uses theoretical modeling involving time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution and analyzing nonadiabatic coupling effects in waveguide QED.
model_or_system: The system is a minimal two-point giant atom coupled to a bidirectional one-dimensional photonic waveguide. Control is achieved by modulating the atomic frequency ($\omega(t)$) or the atom-waveguide coupling strength ($V(t)$).
key_observables: Normalized atomic population $|c_e(t)/c_e(0)|^2$ and outgoing right-propagating photonic intensities $|	ilde{u}_R(z, t)|^2$.
important_parameters: The ramp rate ($\gamma$) of the control knobs (detuning or coupling modulation) is critical; the linear scaling $	ext{P}_{	ext{leak}} \propto \gamma$ is key.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on treating nonadiabatic coupling perturbatively and assumes perfect mode-matching for initial photon capture.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two-knob control mechanism, showing atomic population decay rates versus detuning ramp rate ($\gamma\omega$) or coupling strength ($\Gamma$), and demonstrating the outgoing photonic wavefunctions' dependence on $\Gamma$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the BIC system and its limitations. It then details using two temporal control knobs—atomic-frequency modulation for capture/release, and coupling modulation for gapless tuning. The core results focus on proving adiabaticity despite the lack of a spectral gap.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental issues in open quantum systems by providing a robust protocol to manipulate dark states (BICs) without relying on the standard protection mechanism of spectral gaps, which is highly relevant for photonic quantum information processing.
